prompt: Some governments are moving ministries and other public bodies out of the capital city to smaller towns and regions. Do the advantages of this policy outweigh the disadvantages?
essay:
Relocating a ministry is usually judged by the number of jobs it moves, but the figure that matters is how many decisions move with them. A policy that sends a department's authority to a provincial town is a different undertaking from one that sends only its payroll processing and its call centre, and the balance of advantages and disadvantages differs accordingly.

The advantages are considerable when the move is genuine. A capital that holds most of a country's secure professional jobs drains talent from everywhere else, and a ministry of several thousand people, relocated to a town that has lost its main industry, brings not only salaries but the lawyers, caterers and contractors who serve it. Its officials, living among the people their policies affect, are less likely to design rules that make sense only in the capital. Even the capital benefits, since every office that leaves eases demand for its expensive housing and crowded trains.

The costs are equally real, but they are largely temporary. New buildings must be paid for, and many experienced staff, tied to the capital by a partner's career or a child's schooling, will not move, so the department loses knowledge that may take years to rebuild. These are one-off losses, however, whereas the concentration of opportunity in a single city is a permanent drain. The disadvantage that does not fade is the hollow move, in which the processing work is sent to the regions, the senior posts stay beside the minister, and the town receives low-paid jobs while the country's decisions continue to be made where they always were.

My verdict therefore depends on which of these a government intends. Where whole bodies move, with their leadership, their budgets and the authority to act, the advantages clearly outweigh the disadvantages, because the costs are paid once and the benefits accumulate. Where only the routine work leaves, the policy carries all the expense and disruption of relocation while delivering little of its purpose, and it would be better not to attempt it at all.
title: Moving government offices out of the capital
